title: "Setting up sign-in (OpenID Connect)"
output: rmarkdown::html_document
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = FALSE)
```

A shared atima server does not keep passwords. People sign in through an
identity provider, an organisation that already knows who they are, using
OpenID Connect (OIDC), the standard that "Sign in with ..." buttons use.
This article is for the person who runs the server. It explains what
`auth = "oidc"` does, how to register the server with Globus Auth or ORCID,
every setting involved, how to name administrators, and the things that go
wrong if a setting is changed later. Putting the server behind HTTPS and
running it in a container are covered in
[Running a shared server](server.html).

Sign-in has been tested against a mock provider, in automated tests and by
hand. It has not yet been tested against Globus Auth or ORCID themselves.
Try a sign-in on a test server before you announce yours.


## What `auth = "oidc"` does

- Visitors start as **guests**. A guest is a browser that has not signed
  in. Guests can explore public projects, upload data and save projects.
- A visitor who chooses "Sign in" is sent to the provider, signs in there,
  and is sent back. atima never sees the password they use with the
  provider.
- atima recognises a person by two values the provider vouches for: the
  provider's address (the **issuer**) and the provider's identifier for the
  person (the **`sub`**, short for subject). It never matches people by
  email address or name.

### What atima stores about a person

| Stored | Where it comes from |
|--------|---------------------|
| Issuer and `sub` | The provider, at sign-in. |
| Name, email address, affiliation | The provider, replaced with what it says at each sign-in. ORCID sends no email address and no affiliation. |
| Whether the person is an administrator | The `admins` setting. |
| When the person last used the server | atima. |

In the browser atima sets one cookie, `auth_token`, a random string. The
database keeps only a hash of it (SHA-256), so the database cannot be used
to forge a cookie. The cookie cannot be read by scripts, is not sent with
requests that other sites make, and is marked `Secure` when the site is
served over HTTPS.

atima stores no password and none of the provider's tokens.

### What other people can see of a person

Someone who is signed in and shares a project can search for other people
with accounts. The search, and the list of who has access to a project,
show a person's name, their affiliation, and their email address with part
of it hidden. For someone who signed in with ORCID, which sends no email
address, the ORCID iD is shown instead; an ORCID iD is public by design.
The `sub` of any other provider is never shown. Guests cannot search for
people or see who a project is shared with.


## Before you register

Decide the address people will type, for example
`https://atima.example.org`. This is the server's `public_url`. Sign-in
depends on it in two places:

- The provider sends people back to `<public_url>/auth/callback`, the
  **redirect URL**. You give this URL to the provider when you register,
  and it must match exactly: the scheme (`https`), the host name, the port
  if there is one, and the path. `https://atima.example.org/auth/callback`
  and `https://www.atima.example.org/auth/callback` are different URLs.
- `public_url` must start with `https://`, unless it is a `localhost`
  address used for a trial.

A server uses one provider. Choose it before people start to use the
server (see "Changing the provider later").


## Registering with Globus Auth

[Globus Auth](https://www.globus.org/platform/services/auth) lets people
sign in with the account of their university or institute, and with ORCID
and Google accounts. It is atima's default provider.

1. Sign in at <https://app.globus.org/settings/developers>.
2. Choose to register a **portal or web application that you host**. Do
   not choose a native app or a service account.
3. Put the registration in a Globus project that belongs to your lab or
   group, not to you alone, so that a colleague can manage it later.
4. Set the redirect URL to `https://atima.example.org/auth/callback`, with
   your own host name. Globus accepts only `https://` redirect URLs, with
   one exception: `http://localhost`.
5. If you are asked for scopes, give `openid`, `profile` and `email`.
6. Generate a client secret. Note the client id (a UUID) and the secret;
   the secret is shown once.

Then start the server with:

| Environment variable | Value |
|----------------------|-------|
| `ATIMA_AUTH` | `oidc` |
| `ATIMA_PUBLIC_URL` | `https://atima.example.org` |
| `ATIMA_OIDC_CLIENT_ID` | `<client id>` |
| `ATIMA_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET` | `<client secret>` |

The issuer does not have to be set: the default,
`https://auth.globus.org`, is right.

### Trying it on your own computer first

Because Globus accepts `http://localhost`, you can try sign-in on a laptop
with no HTTPS and no host name. Register a second application (or add a
second redirect URL) with exactly `http://localhost:8080/auth/callback`,
then, in a terminal:

```sh
export ATIMA_OIDC_CLIENT_ID="<client id>"
export ATIMA_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET="<client secret>"
Rscript -e 'atima::run(auth = "oidc", data_dir = tempfile("atima_trial_"))'
```

With `auth = "oidc"`, the default `host` and no `public_url`, atima takes
`http://localhost:8080` as its address. Open exactly that address, not
`http://127.0.0.1:8080`: the browser treats the two as different sites,
and a sign-in started at one cannot finish at the other. The example uses a
temporary data directory so that the trial does not touch your own local
data (see "Moving a local data directory to a shared server").


## Registering with ORCID instead

[ORCID](https://orcid.org) gives every researcher an identifier, the ORCID
iD. Use it as the provider if your users are more likely to have an ORCID
iD than an institute that Globus knows.

1. Sign in at <https://orcid.org>.
2. Open **Developer Tools** in the menu under your name, and register for
   the public API.
3. Add the redirect URI `https://atima.example.org/auth/callback`, with
   your own host name. ORCID accepts only HTTPS in production, and the URI
   must match exactly, host name included.
4. Note the client id and the client secret.

Then start the server with:

| Environment variable | Value |
|----------------------|-------|
| `ATIMA_AUTH` | `oidc` |
| `ATIMA_PUBLIC_URL` | `https://atima.example.org` |
| `ATIMA_OIDC_ISSUER` | `https://orcid.org` |
| `ATIMA_OIDC_CLIENT_ID` | `<client id>` |
| `ATIMA_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET` | `<client secret>` |

What is different with ORCID:

- ORCID sends a name and nothing else: no email address and no
  affiliation. People are told apart by their ORCID iD.
- A person's `sub` is their ORCID iD, for example `0000-0002-1825-0097`
  (ORCID's own example iD).
- ORCID has a sandbox for trying things, at <https://sandbox.orcid.org>,
  with its own accounts and its own registrations. To use it, register
  there and set `ATIMA_OIDC_ISSUER=https://sandbox.orcid.org`. Accounts
  from the sandbox are not the same people as accounts from
  `https://orcid.org`; do not let real users onto a server that points at
  the sandbox.


## Settings

Each setting can be an argument of `atima::run()`, an environment
variable, or an R option (`options(atima.<name> = )`). The first that is
set is used. On a server, environment variables are the usual way.

| Argument | Environment variable | Default | What it does |
|----------|----------------------|---------|--------------|
| `auth` | `ATIMA_AUTH` | `none` | `oidc` switches sign-in on. |
| `host` | `ATIMA_HOST` | `127.0.0.1` | The address to listen on. `0.0.0.0` listens on all interfaces, which a server behind a reverse proxy or in a container needs. |
| `public_url` | `ATIMA_PUBLIC_URL` | `http://localhost:<port>` when `host` is this computer, otherwise required | The address people type, with no path. The redirect URL is this plus `/auth/callback`. |
| `oidc_issuer` | `ATIMA_OIDC_ISSUER` | `https://auth.globus.org` | The provider's issuer URL, exactly as the provider states it. |
| `oidc_client_id` | `ATIMA_OIDC_CLIENT_ID` | none, required | The client id from the registration. |
| `oidc_client_secret` | `ATIMA_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET` | none, required | The client secret from the registration. |
| `admins` | `ATIMA_ADMINS` | not set | The `sub` values of the administrators, separated by commas. See "Administrators". |
| `signin_days` | `ATIMA_SIGNIN_DAYS` | `30` | How long a sign-in lasts. |
| `guest_days` | `ATIMA_GUEST_DAYS` | `30` | A guest who has not visited for this many days is forgotten, with the projects only they could open. |
| `forwarded_proto_header` | `ATIMA_FORWARDED_PROTO_HEADER` | not set | The name of a header in which your reverse proxy says whether the visitor used HTTPS, usually `X-Forwarded-Proto`. Not needed when `public_url` starts with `https://`. If you set it, the proxy must overwrite that header on every request, so that a visitor cannot send their own. |
| `jobs_per_user` | `ATIMA_JOBS_PER_USER` | `16` | The most jobs one person, or one guest, may have waiting or running at once. |
| `operator` | `ATIMA_OPERATOR` | not set | Who runs the server, as the words that finish "This server is run by ...". Shown on the app's "Privacy and terms" page. |
| `contact` | `ATIMA_CONTACT` | not set | How users can reach whoever runs the server: an email address or the `https://` address of a page. Shown on the same page. |

atima reads everything else about the provider (where to send people,
where to exchange the code, which keys sign its tokens) from the
provider's discovery document, at
`<issuer>/.well-known/openid-configuration`. It reads it when the server
starts. If the provider cannot be reached then, the server starts anyway,
prints a warning, writes an `oidc_discovery_failed` line to the log, and
tries again the first time someone signs in.

### Where the client secret belongs

The client secret is a password for your server. Whoever has it can
pretend to be your server to the provider.

- Give it to the server through its environment, or through the secret
  store of whatever runs the server.
- Do not write it in an R script, in a compose file, or in any file that
  is kept in version control.
- atima does not write it to the log and does not pass it to its worker
  processes.
- If it may have leaked, generate a new one at the provider, delete the
  old one there, and restart the server with the new one. Nobody has to
  sign in again because of that.


## Administrators

An administrator can edit and unpublish any public project, and arranges
the collections that public projects are listed under. An administrator
cannot open other people's private projects, and there is no
page for managing users.

Administrators are named by their `sub`, which you can only know after
the person has signed in once:

1. Have the person sign in to the server.
2. Read their `sub` from the database, the file `sqlite.db` in the
   server's data directory:

   ```{r}
   con <- DBI::dbConnect(
     RSQLite::SQLite(), "<data directory>/sqlite.db",
     flags = RSQLite::SQLITE_RO )
   DBI::dbGetQuery(con, "
     SELECT full_name, email, sub FROM users
     WHERE is_guest = 0 AND issuer IS NOT NULL")
   DBI::dbDisconnect(con)
   ```

   For Globus Auth a `sub` is a UUID. For ORCID it is the ORCID iD.
3. Set `ATIMA_ADMINS` to the `sub` values, separated by commas, and
   restart the server:

   ```sh
   ATIMA_ADMINS="<sub of the first administrator>,<sub of the second>"
   ```

4. The person becomes an administrator the next time they sign in. If
   they are signed in already, they sign out and in again.

When `ATIMA_ADMINS` is set, it decides at every sign-in: a person who is
on the list is made an administrator, and a person who is not on it stops
being one. When it is not set, administrators stay as they are in the
database.


## What people who use the server should know

**Signing in lasts `signin_days`.** After 30 days (by default) the browser
has to sign in again. There is no silent renewal. Signing in and signing
out both close the browser's open atima tabs on the server, and unsaved
changes in them are lost, so save first.

**Signing out of atima does not sign out of the provider.** On a shared
computer, sign out of the provider as well, or the next person can sign
straight back in.

**Guests.** A guest's projects are tied to a cookie in their browser. They
are deleted `guest_days` after the guest's last visit, and are lost
earlier if the browser's cookies are cleared. A guest cannot share a
project with a named person, search for people, or publish a project.

**What happens to a guest's data at sign-in.** When a guest signs in from
the same browser, everything they saved as a guest becomes theirs: their
projects, their collections, and the access they had to other projects.
The guest is then deleted. Unsaved changes in the open tab are not carried
over.

**A sign-in must be finished within ten minutes** of choosing "Sign in",
in the same browser. If the server is restarted in between, the person
starts again.

**Public projects are not reviewed.** Anyone who is signed in and can edit
a project can publish it. Administrators can edit or unpublish it
afterwards.

The app has a page, "Privacy and terms", that tells users what the server
stores and for how long. Set `operator` and `contact` so that it says who
runs the server.


## Things that go wrong later

### Changing the provider later

A person is the pair (issuer, `sub`). If you change `oidc_issuer` on a
server that people have already signed in to, every one of them is a
stranger to atima at their next sign-in. They get a new, empty account.
Their old account and its projects are still in the database, but nobody
can sign in to it, and atima has no way to join the two.

This also applies to moving between ORCID's sandbox and ORCID, and to
moving between Globus Auth and ORCID even though Globus lets people sign
in with their ORCID account: the two providers give different `sub`
values for the same person.

A server uses one provider at a time. Choose it before you invite anyone.

### Moving a local data directory to a shared server

A data directory that was used with `auth = "none"` contains one user, the
local owner, who owns every project in it. If you start a server with
`auth = "oidc"` on that directory, those projects still belong to the
local owner, and nobody can sign in as the local owner. The projects are
not deleted, but they are in nobody's project list, and nobody can edit,
share or delete them.

To bring local projects to a shared server, start the shared server on a
new, empty data directory, and upload the projects again: in the local
atima, download each project as a BIOM file, then upload the file to the
shared server after signing in.

The opposite mistake is less harmful. If a shared server's data directory
is opened with `auth = "none"`, people who signed in through a provider
are left as they are.

### The redirect URL does not match

The provider refuses the sign-in, on its own page, with a message about
the redirect URI. Compare the URL registered at the provider with
`<public_url>/auth/callback`, character by character. Common causes are
`http` instead of `https`, a `www.` on one side only, a port on one side
only, and a `public_url` that was changed after registration.

### "Sign-in could not be completed. Please try again."

atima shows this one message whatever the reason, and writes the reason to
the server log, in the `detail` of an `error` line. The usual reasons:

| `detail` in the log | Meaning |
|---------------------|---------|
| `Unknown, reused or expired state.` | The sign-in took more than ten minutes, the server was restarted meanwhile, or the browser's Back button replayed an old sign-in. |
| `The sign-in was not started by this browser.` | The sign-in began at one address and ended at another (for example `127.0.0.1` and `localhost`), or cookies are blocked. |
| `The provider refused the code (HTTP ..., ...).` | The provider did not accept the request, and its error code is in the brackets. `invalid_client` means that the client id or secret is wrong. |
| `The ID token has expired (exp).` or `... is not valid yet (nbf).` | The server's clock is wrong. |

### The provider's issuer does not match

At start-up atima prints that the provider "says its issuer is ..., not
...". Set `oidc_issuer` to exactly the value the provider states, without
a trailing slash unless the provider's has one.

### The provider is slow or down

A sign-in waits for the provider for at most ten seconds per call, and
then fails with the message above. The server keeps answering everyone
else meanwhile. (One short exception: the first sign-in after a start, or
after the provider changed its signing keys, fetches the keys while other
requests wait.) People who are already signed in are not affected by a
provider that is down, until their sign-in runs out.
